name: Ice Magic
oracle_text:
Tiered (Choose one additional cost.)
• Blizzard — {0} — Return target creature to its owner's hand.
• Blizzara — {2} — Target creature's owner puts it on their choice of the top or bottom of their library.
• Blizzaga — {5}{U} — Target creature's owner shuffles it into their library.
blocked_sentences: • Blizzard — {0} — Return target creature to its owner's hand.
• Blizzara — {2} — Target creature's owner puts it on their choice of the top or bottom of their library.
• Blizzaga — {5}{U} — Target creature's owner shuffles it into their library.

needs.what: a card-level additional cost with alternatives -- an `additional_cost_options` list of whole costs (each a cost_keys node; here {"mana": "{0}"}, {"mana": "{2}"}, {"mana": "{5}{U}"}) of which exactly one must be chosen and paid while casting, with the chosen index recorded on the spell so the effect tree can branch on it. NOTE FOR WHOEVER BUILDS THIS: Ice Magic's three tiers are genuinely DISTINCT EFFECTS, not one effect with a scaling number the way Fire Magic's are (1/2/3 damage to each creature). Blizzard bounces to hand, Blizzara puts the creature on the top or bottom of its owner's library at that owner's choice, Blizzaga shuffles it into its owner's library -- three different ops with three different destinations. So the tier choice cannot be modelled as an `amount` that varies with `additional_paid`; it must select a whole branch of the effect tree. The mechanism therefore has to be the general one: the caster picks an option as part of casting (locked in on announcement, part of the spell's total cost, visible to cost-watching effects), and the paid option binds the effect -- either by letting a top-level `choose_mode` mode be legal only when its own option was the one paid, or by a new `condition`/`value` leaf such as `cost_option_chosen` that an `if` can read. All three of Ice Magic's tiers also TARGET a creature, so the existing mode-owned target rule (a target spec carrying its owning `mode` index) must keep working here -- one target spec per tier, declared only when that tier is the one paid for. Fire Magic's tiers target nothing, so Ice Magic is the card that exercises the targeting half of this feature.
needs.why_existing_wont_do: `additional_cost` is a single fixed price every cast must pay -- it can express {0} or {2} or {5}{U} but never a choice among them. `additional_optional`/`kicker` is one yes/no price: two outcomes, not three named tiers. `additional_repeatable`/`multikicker` is N repetitions of one price, and cannot reach {0}, {2} and {5}{U} as steps of a single cost (the third is not even a generic multiple -- it adds a coloured {U}). `alternative_cost`, `evoke` and `overload` each replace the mana cost with exactly one substitute rather than adding a chosen extra. On the effect side `choose_mode` carries only chooser/count/modes/once_each/or_more/up_to/up_to_if -- no per-mode cost key at all -- so writing the three bullets as three free modes would print a {1}{U} instant that shuffles any creature into its owner's library, which is strictly better than the card. The `may`-with-`pay` dodge moves payment to resolution, so the tier would be chosen after the spell is on the stack, the total cost paid would be wrong, and the caster could hold the choice open past responses. `additional_paid` can read how much extra was paid but nothing offers a fixed menu of extra prices at cast time, so there is no value for it to read -- and even with it, a number cannot pick between `return_to_hand` and `put_on_top`.

expressible_today.• Blizzard — {0} — Return target creatur: YES. `return_to_hand` takes `objects`, so this is `{"op": "return_to_hand", "objects": {"target": "creature"}}` with a card-level target of kind creature. Nothing here is missing but the cost menu.
expressible_today.• Blizzara — {2} — Target creature's own: NO -- blocked a second time, independently of `tiered`. `put_on_top` (options: from_top, objects) is the only op that moves an object to a library position, and it reaches the TOP only. There is no put-on-bottom for an arbitrary object: the only bottom-of-library movement in `op_options` is `look_at_top`'s `rest_to_bottom` and `reveal_until`'s `rest_to_bottom`, both of which dispose of cards the op itself revealed off the top of a library, not a permanent on the battlefield. `put_on_top` also has no `chooser`, so even a top/bottom pair of ops could not hand the decision to the creature's owner rather than the caster. See the second need below.
expressible_today.• Blizzaga — {5}{U} — Target creature's: MOSTLY. `search_library` is the wrong direction (a tutor; its `shuffle` flag shuffles only the searching player's library) and there is no `put_into_library` op, but `put_on_top` followed by `shuffle` is the standard composition and is the shape the engine already has: `[{"op": "put_on_top", "objects": {"target": "creature"}}, {"op": "shuffle", "player": <that creature's owner>}]`. One thing to confirm when building: `shuffle` takes only `player`, and the shuffling player here is the TARGET's owner, not the caster -- if `player` cannot name the owner of a targeted object, this tier needs that reference (or a `shuffle_into_library` op) as well.

needs.what: a way to put a targeted object on the BOTTOM of its owner's library, and a `chooser` on that decision so the owner picks top or bottom. Cleanest form: extend `put_on_top` with a `bottom: true` (or a `position: "top"|"bottom"|"owner_choice"` key) plus a `chooser` naming who decides -- "puts it on their choice of the top or bottom of their library" is then one op with chooser set to the object's owner. Needed by the whole Blizzara/Condemn/Griptide family, not just this card.
needs.why_existing_wont_do: `put_on_top` is the only op in `op_options` that puts an object into a library, and its options are just `from_top` and `objects` -- top only, no bottom, no chooser. `look_at_top` and `reveal_until` each have a `rest_to_bottom`, but that only disposes of cards those ops themselves looked at off a library's top; neither can take a battlefield permanent. `choose_mode` does have a `chooser`, so a two-mode choose_mode could hand the decision to the opponent, but its bottom branch still has no op to call.
